## Web Development Company in Pune: What 2026's New Baseline CSS Features Mean for Your Website Build

Four CSS features — `@starting-style`, `contrast-color()`, `field-sizing: content`, and the `:open` selector — crossed into cross-browser Baseline status through 2026, and together they remove a surprising amount of JavaScript that websites have carried for years just to animate a modal, resize a textarea, or check a color's contrast. For a business owner briefing a web development company in Pune on a new build or a redesign, the practical upshot is simple: interactions that used to need a animation library, an autosize plugin, and manual color QA can now be handled by the browser itself, which means less code to maintain and fewer places for bugs to hide. This article walks through what each feature actually does, where it helps on a real Indian business site — from a checkout drawer to an NGO donation form — and where the caveats still apply.

## What "Baseline 2026" Actually Means for a Website Build

Baseline is the practical answer to "can I use this yet?" — it tracks when a web platform feature works consistently across Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge, rather than relying on a single browser's roadmap. A feature reaches "Newly Available" once it ships in the current stable release of all major engines, and "Widely Available" roughly 30 months later, once older installed browser versions have mostly aged out. That distinction matters more than most marketing copy about CSS suggests, because "Newly Available" is not the same guarantee as "safe to depend on for every visitor." It means the current version of every major browser supports it — not that every phone in your customer base is running that current version.

2026 has been an unusually productive year for this list. Alongside the four features covered in depth here, `@scope` — a way to limit a block of CSS rules to a specific subtree of the page instead of leaking into everything below it — also reached Baseline this year, which is genuinely useful for teams maintaining large component libraries or WordPress theme child-overrides without CSS specificity wars. We've also covered the `:has()` selector reaching Baseline in a [previous look at CSS selectors in 2026](/blog/website-designer-pune-css-has-selector-2026), which is worth reading alongside this piece since `:has()` and `:open` solve a similar class of problem: replacing JavaScript state-tracking with native CSS matching. None of this is exotic committee work — it's the browser vendors converging on patterns that developers had already been faking with JavaScript for a decade, and formalizing them so every site can drop the workaround.

## @starting-style: Entry Animations Without a JavaScript Timing Hack

The oldest annoyance in CSS transitions is this: you cannot transition an element's appearance the moment it goes from `display: none` to visible, because the browser applies the "after" styles instantly and there's no "before" state to animate from. Developers have worked around this for years with `setTimeout` calls, a forced reflow trick (reading `offsetHeight` to flush styles), or by reaching for a JavaScript animation library just to sequence a fade-in correctly. `@starting-style` finally gives CSS its own answer: you define what the element should look like in its starting state, and the browser handles the transition from there — no timing hack required.

### Where this actually helps on an Indian business site

Two patterns come up constantly in the kind of client work we do. The first is a cart drawer or mobile navigation panel that slides in from the side — previously built either with a CSS class toggled by JavaScript on a delay, or with a full animation library dependency just for one interaction. With `@starting-style`, the drawer can transition its `transform` and `opacity` from a defined starting state the instant it's added to the DOM, with a plain CSS transition and no library. The second, and one we see often given our NGO client base, is a donation modal or "thank you" confirmation overlay: it needs to fade and scale in cleanly rather than snapping into view, because a jarring pop-in undermines the sense of trust you want at the exact moment someone is entering payment details. Getting that polish previously meant either accepting the abrupt native behaviour or writing (and maintaining) animation JavaScript for what is, conceptually, a two-line CSS transition.

It's worth being direct about the limit here too: `@starting-style` only defines the starting point of a transition — it doesn't replace complex choreographed animations, staggered lists, or gesture-driven interactions, which still warrant a proper animation approach. Its win is specifically the class of "element appears, and I want that appearance to be smooth" interactions that make up the bulk of everyday UI polish.

## field-sizing: content — Textareas and Inputs That Grow With What You Type

Every developer who has built a comment box, a contact form, or a checkout notes field has written some version of the same JavaScript: listen for `input` events, read `scrollHeight`, reset the height to `auto` first to avoid it only growing and never shrinking, then set the new height. It works, but it's brittle — it has to be re-run on paste, on programmatic value changes, on window resize with responsive font sizes, and it typically needs a debounce to avoid layout thrashing on every keystroke. `field-sizing: content` does the same job as a single CSS declaration: the textarea or input grows (and shrinks) to fit its content automatically, with no listener code at all.

### Concrete uses on a contact or checkout form

Think about the message field on a [contact-us page](/contact-us): most visitors write two lines, but a handful write a detailed paragraph describing exactly what they need. A fixed-height box either wastes space for the two-line replies or clips and forces scrolling for the long ones — `field-sizing: content` lets one field handle both gracefully. The same applies to a delivery-notes or gift-message field on a checkout flow, an area we build often as part of [checkout system work](/services/checkout-system): a growing textarea removes the awkward internal scrollbar that shows up on mobile Safari when a fixed-height field is nearly full, which is a small thing but a noticeably rough edge when a customer is mid-purchase.

Does this fully replace the JavaScript autosize libraries in use today? Mostly, for the common case — but not universally yet, which we cover directly in the FAQ below, since it's one of the more practical questions a business owner should ask their developer before ripping out an existing library.

## contrast-color(): Automatic Legible Text Against Any Background

This is the feature with the most direct accessibility payoff. `contrast-color()` is a CSS function that looks at a given background color and automatically returns whichever text color — typically black or white, or a color from a palette you supply — will read most legibly against it, aiming to satisfy WCAG contrast guidelines. It shipped in Chrome 147 (April 2026), Firefox 146, and Safari 26.0, and reached Baseline "Newly Available" status on April 10, 2026, according to the Baseline feature tracker.

### Why this matters beyond "nice to have"

Any site where color is dynamic — set by a CMS field, a user's brand-color picker, a category tag system, or a badge component that inherits a brand color per client — has almost certainly shipped a contrast bug at some point. A designer picks a brand palette that looks fine on a mockup, an editor later adds a new category color in the CMS, and nobody re-checks that white text still reads clearly on it. `contrast-color()` removes that entire failure class for text-on-background pairings: instead of hardcoding `color: white` and hoping every future background stays dark enough, you write `color: contrast-color(var(--bg))` and the browser recalculates the right choice every time the background changes. For an NGO donation platform showing dozens of campaign-specific accent colors, or a multi-brand client portal, that's a meaningful reduction in manual QA — the kind of accessibility ground we also cover in our piece on [Core Web Vitals and WCAG accessibility for Pune-built sites](/blog/website-accessibility-core-web-vitals-designer-pune-2026).

The honest caveat, and one worth repeating to any developer proposing to use this today: "Newly Available" as of April 2026 is not "Widely Available" — that status for `contrast-color()` isn't projected until October 2028, once older browser versions have largely cycled out of use. In practice that means a competent build still needs a fallback color declared before the `contrast-color()` line, so browsers that don't yet recognize the function simply use the fallback instead of breaking. It is a strong tool for reducing contrast bugs going forward — it is not a substitute for testing on the actual browser versions your visitor base runs today.

## :open — Styling Native Accordions and Popovers With Pure CSS

The `:open` selector matches any element currently in an "open" state: an expanded native `<details>` element, a visible `<dialog>`, or a popover shown via the Popover API. Before this, styling the open state of these elements meant either watching for the browser's own toggle events in JavaScript and applying a class, or building the entire accordion/popover behaviour from scratch with a JS state library rather than using the native HTML elements at all. `:open` lets you write the open-state styling directly in CSS and let the native element's own state drive it.

### A cleaner path for FAQ accordions and menus

An FAQ accordion built on native `<details>`/`<summary>` elements is already good for accessibility and SEO out of the box — screen readers understand it natively, and it works with JavaScript disabled — but developers have often avoided it because styling the expanded state cleanly required extra JavaScript. `:open` removes that trade-off: you get the native semantics and the custom visual polish (rotating an arrow icon, changing a background tint, animating the height) from CSS alone. The same logic applies to a popover-based navigation menu or a "more options" dropdown — no state library, no manual click-outside-to-close JavaScript reimplementation, because the Popover API and `:open` already handle it. This pairs naturally with the anchor positioning and container query features we detailed in [our earlier piece on positioning tooltips and dropdowns without JavaScript](/blog/website-designer-pune-anchor-positioning-container-queries-2026) — between the two, a large share of what used to require a UI component library is now achievable with native HTML and CSS.

## Choosing a Web Development Company in Pune That Actually Uses These Features

This is where the decision becomes practical rather than academic. A web development company in Pune that is still hand-rolling autosize JavaScript for every textarea, or shipping a full animation library dependency for a single modal fade-in, isn't necessarily doing bad work — but it is very likely carrying more code, more bundle weight, and more edge-case bugs than a build that leans on these native features where they fit. When you're briefing a [website design and development project](/services/website-creation), it's fair to ask directly: does the team know which of these features apply to this specific build, and do they have a plan for the browsers that don't yet support them? A team that answers vaguely, or claims every visitor is already on a fully updated browser, hasn't thought it through — the honest answer always involves a fallback strategy, not a blanket assumption.

It's equally fair to push back on a developer who insists on rebuilding everything with these features immediately, everywhere, regardless of what your actual visitor analytics show about browser and device versions. The right approach is targeted: use `@starting-style` for meaningful entry animations, use `field-sizing: content` for growing text fields, use `:open` for native accordions and popovers, and use `contrast-color()` for dynamically-set colors — while keeping the previous JavaScript-based approach in place for anything where fallback behaviour genuinely matters. That's a judgment call a competent developer makes per feature, not a switch flipped for the whole site at once.

## Progressive Enhancement: How This Should Actually Ship

None of these four features should be treated as a hard dependency on a client-facing build, and this is the single most important operational point in this article. The correct pattern for all of them is progressive enhancement: write the fallback first — a fixed-height textarea, a static modal, a plain text color, a JavaScript-toggled accordion class — and then layer the new CSS on top using `@supports` feature queries where the behaviour differs meaningfully, so unsupported browsers get a working (if slightly less polished) experience rather than a broken one. This is exactly how `contrast-color()` needs to be shipped today given its "Newly Available" status, and it's good practice for the other three regardless of their support numbers, because older Android devices running outdated system WebViews — common on budget phones still active across Tier 2 and Tier 3 Indian markets — won't recognize every one of these features even after "Baseline" status is reached in the major desktop browsers.

Practically, this means a developer should be checking real analytics for your specific site's browser and OS breakdown before deciding how aggressively to adopt any of these, rather than assuming Baseline status alone is a green light. A B2B SaaS dashboard used mostly on recent laptops can adopt faster than a public-facing donation form that needs to work reliably on whatever phone a first-time donor happens to be holding.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Do these new CSS features work in older browsers, or on older phones with outdated WebViews?

Not universally, and that's expected rather than a flaw. Baseline status means the current stable release of every major browser engine supports the feature — it does not mean every device already in use has updated to that version. Older Android phones running outdated system WebViews, and any browser that hasn't been updated in a year or more, may not recognize some or all of these features yet. That's exactly why a competent build wraps each of them in a fallback (a plain color, a fixed-height field, a JavaScript-toggled class) so unsupported devices still get a working experience, just without the extra polish — nothing breaks, it simply looks and behaves the way it did before these features existed.

### Does field-sizing: content fully replace the JavaScript autosize libraries developers use today?

For the common case, yes — but not universally yet, so it's not a blanket replacement on every project as of today. Where `field-sizing: content` is supported (Chrome 123+, Firefox 152+, Safari 26.2+, Edge 123+), it removes the need for scroll-height listeners and manual resize logic entirely, and it's typically smoother because it's handled by the browser's own layout engine rather than reacting after the fact in JavaScript. The sensible approach right now is to use it as the primary method with a `@supports` fallback to the existing JavaScript autosize behaviour for browsers that don't yet recognize the CSS property, rather than deleting the library outright — which is a decision your developer should make explicitly, not by default.

### Is contrast-color() the same thing as choosing brand colors — does it replace a designer's color decisions?

No — it's a safety mechanism for text legibility, not a color-choosing tool for a brand palette. A designer still chooses the brand colors, the accent tones, the overall visual identity — `contrast-color()` only decides, at the moment a background color is applied, whether black or white (or a supplied alternative) text will read more clearly against it. It's most valuable specifically where the background color is dynamic or unpredictable at design time: a CMS-driven category color, a per-campaign accent on a donation platform, or a user-set theme color — situations where nobody can manually verify every possible combination in advance. For a fixed, designer-chosen palette, manual contrast checking during design remains entirely appropriate.

### Will using @starting-style entry animations cause problems for users who have "reduced motion" turned on?

Only if the developer forgets to account for it, which is a general animation best practice rather than something specific to this feature. Any transition or animation — whether built with `@starting-style`, plain CSS transitions, or a JavaScript library — should be wrapped in a `prefers-reduced-motion` media query check, so users who've enabled that operating system accessibility setting see the content appear instantly rather than sliding, fading, or scaling in. `@starting-style` doesn't change this obligation one way or the other; it just makes the animation itself easier to write correctly, so there's less excuse for skipping the reduced-motion fallback.

### Do I need to rebuild my existing website to start using these features, or can a developer add them incrementally?

No rebuild is needed for any of these four. Each one is additive: a growing textarea, an automatic contrast fix, a native accordion style, or a smoother modal fade-in can all be added to an existing page's CSS without touching the surrounding markup, layout, or JavaScript logic that already works. The realistic path is incremental — a developer identifies a handful of components where one of these features removes real complexity (a form, a modal, an FAQ block) and updates those specific pieces during ordinary maintenance work, rather than treating this as a reason for a full redesign.

## Where to Go From Here

Adopting features like `@starting-style`, `field-sizing: content`, `contrast-color()`, and `:open` is less about chasing what's new in CSS and more about knowing which of them genuinely simplifies a specific part of your site — which is the kind of judgment call we make daily across the [website design and development](/services/website-creation) work we do for businesses and NGOs in Pune, including the donation and checkout flows built through our [checkout system service](/services/checkout-system), where a clean entry animation on a payment step or a form field that grows naturally with a donor's message genuinely affects how trustworthy the experience feels. Since 500+ non-profit websites have gone through our team, we've seen firsthand how much manual color and layout QA these features can remove from a donation platform carrying dozens of campaign-specific brand colors — reducing that maintenance burden also frees up attention for the [SEO work](/services/seo) that actually brings donors and customers to the site in the first place. If you're planning a new build or reviewing whether your current site's development approach is keeping up, [get in touch through our contact page](/contact-us) and we'll walk through what's actually worth adopting for your specific traffic and browser mix.
